I've been farming this land in Quzhou for 35 years. I know what works here on the North China Plain. My wheat and maize go on the same 8 mu — wheat in autumn, maize right after I cut the wheat in June. That rotation is what my father did and what everyone around me does. The other 2.1 mu I keep for cotton, though it's getting harder with my son working in the city and my wife doing factory shifts. Less hands means I can't expand the cotton, but I won't drop it either — when the price is good it still pays.

For wheat, I'll rotary-till after the maize comes out, then sow around October 10th. I use improved seed — I buy from the same village supplier every year, he stocks Jimai varieties that do well here. I'll water four times: before sowing to settle the bed, once in early winter to protect the roots from frost, again at jointing, and once more at heading. My neighbor skips the winter water but I've seen his crop suffer in dry years. Fertilizer goes in at sowing — compound fertilizer — and I top-dress urea at jointing. Three pesticide passes: herbicide in early spring, a fungicide spray at heading for rust and powdery mildew, and I watch for aphids near grain fill.

For summer maize, I seed straight into the wheat stubble right after harvest — no tillage. Saves me two or three days of work when I'm also managing the cotton. I use hybrid seed, same as always. I'll irrigate at emergence if it's dry, again at tasseling, and once more if the ears are filling and it hasn't rained. Two pesticide passes — herbicide early and one for stem borer.

Cotton is the exhausting one. I plough in spring, transplant seedlings in early May. I'll water four times through the summer and spray six times — the bollworm and aphids don't rest. But I use hybrid Bt cotton so I save on two or three of those sprays compared to old varieties.
